difficultyReason: Two-premise argument with several topically related distractors. The gap between the clinical evidence and the conclusion about drug efficacy requires ruling out a confounding explanation. Negation test is decisive but requires careful re-reading.
stimulus: Physician: In a recent clinical trial, patients with chronic migraines who took the new drug valzenide reported a 60 percent reduction in headache frequency. Patients in the control group, who received a placebo, reported only a 15 percent reduction. We can therefore conclude that valzenide is genuinely effective at reducing migraine frequency.
questionStem: The physician's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Valzenide has no significant side effects that would discourage patients from taking it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The patients who took valzenide did not also make lifestyle changes that the control group did not make.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Placebo effects are never observed in trials involving chronic pain conditions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Valzenide will produce similarly large reductions in headache frequency in all future patients.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The clinical trial was conducted at multiple hospitals rather than a single facility.

explanations.correct: The argument infers that valzenide itself caused the superior reduction. If the valzenide group also made beneficial lifestyle changes the control group did not, those changes — not the drug — could explain the difference. Negating B (the valzenide group did make such changes) destroys the causal inference, making B necessary.
explanations.A: Side effects concern tolerability and patient compliance, not whether the observed reduction is attributable to the drug versus a confound. Out of scope for this causal inference.
explanations.B: Correct. This is the necessary assumption — it rules out a key confounding variable that would undermine the attribution of the reduction to valzenide.
explanations.C: Too strong. The argument doesn't need placebo effects to be impossible — it only needs the drug group's additional improvement over the placebo group to be due to the drug, not a separate cause.
explanations.D: This is a sufficient-condition trap. The argument concludes only that valzenide is effective, not that it works universally in all future patients. This goes beyond what the argument requires.
explanations.E: The number of facilities is irrelevant to the causal inference drawn from the trial's comparative results.

difficultyReason: Economics domain argument with a plausible financial conclusion and several traps mimicking real economic reasoning. The necessary assumption links the premise about consumer behavior to the policy conclusion without overreaching.
stimulus: Economist: A proposed tariff on imported steel would raise the price of domestic automobiles, since steel is a primary input in automobile manufacturing. Higher automobile prices would cause consumers to defer vehicle purchases. Therefore, the tariff would reduce employment in the domestic automobile industry.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the economist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The domestic steel industry would not hire enough new workers to offset any job losses in the automobile industry.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Automobile manufacturers would not offset higher steel costs by reducing executive compensation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reduced consumer demand for automobiles would lead manufacturers to cut production and, consequently, employment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The proposed tariff would be higher than any tariff previously imposed on imported steel.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Consumers who defer vehicle purchases would eventually buy automobiles once prices stabilize.

explanations.correct: The argument moves from 'consumers defer purchases' to 'employment falls.' That step requires that manufacturers respond to lower demand by cutting production and workers. Negate C — reduced demand does NOT lead to production and employment cuts — and the employment conclusion becomes unsupported.
explanations.A: This concerns a net employment effect across industries, which goes beyond the argument's scope. The economist concludes only about automobile industry employment, not economy-wide employment.
explanations.B: Even if manufacturers absorbed costs through executive pay cuts, prices could still rise and consumers could still defer purchases, supporting the chain. This is not a required link.
explanations.C: Correct. This supplies the missing causal bridge between deferred purchases and reduced employment.
explanations.D: The tariff's magnitude relative to past tariffs is irrelevant; the argument only requires that this tariff raises prices enough to defer purchases.
explanations.E: What consumers eventually do is irrelevant to whether employment falls in the near term as a result of deferred purchases.

difficultyReason: Environmental science argument with a plausible conservation conclusion. Two distractors are close cousins of the correct answer, requiring careful negation testing to distinguish the bridge assumption from mere strengtheners.
stimulus: Conservation biologist: Satellite tracking data show that the migratory routes of monarch butterflies have shifted northward by an average of 200 kilometers over the past three decades. During the same period, the average temperature of the butterflies' traditional wintering grounds increased by 1.8 degrees Celsius. We conclude that rising temperatures in the wintering grounds caused the butterflies to shift their routes northward.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No other significant environmental changes occurred in the butterflies' wintering grounds over the past three decades.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Monarch butterflies are capable of detecting small changes in ambient temperature.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The northward route shift was not caused primarily by changes in the butterflies' summer breeding grounds rather than in their wintering grounds.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rising temperatures in the wintering grounds have also affected other migratory insect species.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Monarch butterfly populations have remained stable over the past three decades.

explanations.correct: The argument attributes the route shift specifically to temperature changes in the wintering grounds. If the shift was primarily caused by changes in the summer breeding grounds instead, the conclusion is unsupported. Negating C directly undermines the causal attribution the argument makes.
explanations.A: Too strong. The argument doesn't require that no other changes occurred — only that the temperature change in the wintering grounds was the cause. Other changes could exist without defeating the argument.
explanations.B: Temperature detection ability is a mechanistic detail not invoked in the argument. The argument infers causation from correlation, so this is out of scope.
explanations.C: Correct. This rules out the most direct alternative causal explanation — that breeding-ground changes, not wintering-ground temperature, drove the shift.
explanations.D: Other species' responses are irrelevant to this argument about monarch butterflies specifically.
explanations.E: Population stability is not a premise or a required bridge in this causal argument about migratory routes.

difficultyReason: Law domain argument with a structural gap between legal precedent and its application. Distractors include a reversed-direction trap and a scope-shift trap, requiring careful attention to what the argument actually needs.
stimulus: Attorney: In Hartwell v. Crane, the court held that a contractor is liable for structural defects that arise from deviating from approved building plans. Our client, a homeowner, discovered that the contractor deviated from the approved plans during construction of her foundation. Therefore, the contractor is liable for the foundation defects she has experienced.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the attorney's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The foundation defects would not have occurred if the contractor had followed the approved plans.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The contractor was aware of the approved building plans at the time of construction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hartwell v. Crane is the most important precedent governing contractor liability in this jurisdiction.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No court in this jurisdiction has issued a ruling that contradicts the holding in Hartwell v. Crane.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The homeowner discovered the foundation defects within the statute of limitations for construction claims.

explanations.correct: The precedent establishes liability for defects that 'arise from' deviating from plans. The argument assumes the deviation caused the defects. If the defects would have occurred even with full compliance, the deviation did not cause them, and the precedent does not apply. Negating A — the defects would have occurred regardless — collapses the argument.
explanations.A: Correct. The causal link between the deviation and the defects is the necessary bridge between the precedent and the conclusion.
explanations.B: The precedent's holding does not require knowledge of the plans as an element of liability — it only requires deviation and resulting defects. Contractor awareness is not invoked.
explanations.C: Too strong and out of scope. The argument only needs Hartwell v. Crane to apply, not to be the most important precedent.
explanations.D: Whether contradicting rulings exist is not addressed in the argument. The attorney may simply be applying Hartwell v. Crane as written without needing to establish it is uncontradicted.
explanations.E: The statute of limitations is a procedural issue not raised in the argument's premises or conclusion.

difficultyReason: Technology domain with a policy conclusion. Multiple distractors appear relevant but either go too far or miss the specific gap. The necessary assumption is defensive — it rules out an alternative explanation for the observed data.
stimulus: Software engineer: Our analysis shows that since the company deployed the new firewall system six months ago, the number of successful cyberattacks on company servers has dropped by 80 percent. The firewall system is therefore responsible for this dramatic improvement in our network security.
questionStem: The engineer's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The new firewall system is more sophisticated than any competing product currently on the market.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The company did not implement other significant security measures at the same time it deployed the firewall.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cyberattacks on companies in the same industry did not also decrease by a similar percentage during the same period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The firewall system has never failed to block an attempted intrusion since its deployment.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The employees who manage the firewall system received adequate training before it was deployed.

explanations.correct: The argument attributes the 80% reduction to the firewall. If the company simultaneously deployed other major security measures, those measures — not the firewall alone — could explain the drop. Negating B destroys the causal attribution, making it a necessary assumption.
explanations.A: The firewall's market ranking is irrelevant to whether it caused the observed improvement. Out of scope.
explanations.B: Correct. This rules out confounding simultaneous interventions that would undermine attributing the improvement specifically to the firewall.
explanations.C: An industry-wide decline would weaken the argument, but the argument does not require that no such decline occurred — only that the firewall caused this company's drop. This answer goes further than necessary.
explanations.D: Too strong. The argument doesn't require the firewall to have a perfect record — only that it is responsible for the overall 80% reduction.
explanations.E: Employee training is a background condition not invoked as a premise, and its adequacy is not a bridge required for the causal inference.

difficultyReason: History domain with an archaeological inference. One distractor is a shift-in-subject trap; another is a reversed-direction trap. The correct answer fills a specific evidentiary gap without over-proving the conclusion.
stimulus: Historian: Excavations at the Veralian settlement uncovered a bronze figurine depicting a seated ruler wearing a distinctive crescent-shaped crown. Contemporaneous inscriptions found at three nearby sites refer to a king whose title translates as 'Wearer of the Moon.' We therefore conclude that the figurine represents this king.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the historian's argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The crescent-shaped crown depicted on the figurine was not a purely decorative motif used on figurines representing multiple rulers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Veralian settlement was the capital city of the kingdom ruled by the king titled 'Wearer of the Moon.'

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bronze figurines were produced exclusively to commemorate ruling monarchs in the region.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The inscriptions at the nearby sites were composed during the reign of the king they describe.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No other rulers in the region wore a crescent-shaped crown during the same period.

explanations.correct: The argument uses the crescent crown as the identifying link between the figurine and the king titled 'Wearer of the Moon.' If the crescent crown was a generic decorative motif applied to figurines of many rulers, the crown does not specifically identify this king. Negating A — the crown was a common decorative motif — undermines the identification, making A necessary.
explanations.A: Correct. If the crown is non-distinctive, the inference from crown to specific king collapses.
explanations.B: The settlement's status as a capital is not required. A figurine depicting the king could be found at a non-capital site. This is out of scope for the narrow identification argument.
explanations.C: Too strong. The argument only needs this figurine to represent a ruler; it does not need bronze figurines to exclusively represent monarchs.
explanations.D: When the inscriptions were composed matters for historical context but is not a bridge in the argument's inference. The inscriptions' content — not their date of composition — is used as evidence.
explanations.E: Too strong. The argument needs only that the crescent crown is distinctively associated with this king, not that absolutely no other ruler ever wore one. Answer A captures this more precisely.

difficultyReason: Ethics/policy domain with a normative argument. The argument moves from a descriptive premise to a prescriptive conclusion, and the necessary assumption is the normative bridge. Distractors include a too-strong answer and an out-of-scope distractor.
stimulus: Policy analyst: City residents consistently report that they feel less safe in neighborhoods where street lighting has been reduced as part of budget cuts. Since people's sense of personal safety is a legitimate component of their well-being, the city should restore street lighting to previous levels in those neighborhoods.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the analyst's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Restoring street lighting would not create new public safety hazards, such as increased pedestrian traffic late at night.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The city's budget cuts were not justified by a genuine fiscal emergency.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Restoring the street lighting would actually improve residents' sense of safety in those neighborhoods.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The city has an obligation to take reasonable steps to protect the well-being of its residents.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduced street lighting has caused an increase in the actual rate of violent crime in those neighborhoods.

explanations.correct: The argument moves from 'sense of safety is part of well-being' to 'the city should restore lighting.' That prescriptive conclusion requires a bridge norm: that the city has an obligation to act on residents' well-being. Without D, the descriptive premise generates no policy obligation. Negating D — the city has no such obligation — leaves the 'should' conclusion unsupported.
explanations.A: Potential new hazards could weaken the argument, but the argument does not need to pre-empt every possible objection to be a valid inference. This is a strengthener, not a necessary assumption.
explanations.B: Whether budget cuts were justified concerns the legitimacy of the cuts, not whether restoring lighting is obligatory. Out of scope for this normative inference.
explanations.C: The argument already premises that residents feel unsafe due to reduced lighting. Restoring it is assumed to address that — but this connection is relatively obvious and is not the core normative gap. The bigger gap is why the city is obligated to act at all.
explanations.D: Correct. This is the normative bridge linking 'residents' well-being is harmed' to 'the city should act.'
explanations.E: The argument is explicitly about perceived safety, not actual crime rates. Introducing actual crime rates shifts the subject entirely.

difficultyReason: Linguistics domain with an inference about language origins. The argument contains a subtle gap between structural similarity and shared origin. Distractors include a reversed-direction trap and a scope-shift trap.
stimulus: Linguist: The Darvanic languages of the northern coast and the Solven languages spoken 800 kilometers inland share a remarkably similar system of grammatical case markers — identical in form and function across 14 distinct cases. This degree of similarity cannot be attributed to coincidence. Therefore, the Darvanic and Solven languages must share a common ancestral language.
questionStem: The linguist's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Darvanic and Solven languages have been spoken in their current geographic locations for at least 2,000 years.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The case marker system could not have spread from one language family to the other through prolonged contact and borrowing.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A common ancestral language would have had at least 14 grammatical cases.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Grammatical case systems are more resistant to change over time than vocabulary.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No living speakers of the proposed common ancestral language exist today.

explanations.correct: The argument rules out coincidence as an explanation and concludes common ancestry. But there is another alternative: language contact and borrowing. If the case markers spread from one family to the other through sustained contact, shared ancestry is not required. Negating B — contact-and-borrowing could explain the similarity — destroys the inference to common ancestry.
explanations.A: Geographic history is not invoked as a premise; the argument relies on structural similarity, not location duration. Out of scope.
explanations.B: Correct. This eliminates the primary alternative explanation — contact diffusion — without which the argument's conclusion does not follow.
explanations.C: Reversed-direction trap. The argument concludes that the languages share an ancestor; it does not require the ancestor to have had a specific number of cases. The number of cases in the descendant languages does not constrain what the ancestor must have had.
explanations.D: The relative stability of case systems is a background linguistic assumption, but the argument relies on the similarity itself, not on whether case systems are especially stable. This is not a required bridge.
explanations.E: The existence or non-existence of living speakers of a proto-language is irrelevant to whether the proto-language existed and gave rise to these two families.

difficultyReason: Arts domain with an attribution argument. The gap is evidentiary: the argument needs a connection between the observed technique and the specific artist. One distractor is too strong; another is a subject-shift trap.
stimulus: Art historian: A recently discovered oil painting depicts a coastal landscape in an unattributed style. Scientific analysis reveals that the painting uses a distinctive layering technique — applying translucent glazes over an opaque white ground — that Flemish master Pieter Vandermeer used exclusively in his authenticated works from the 1640s. We conclude that Vandermeer painted this coastal landscape.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the art historian's argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Vandermeer painted at least one other coastal landscape during the 1640s.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No other painter working in the 1640s used the same distinctive layering technique as Vandermeer.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Scientific analysis of oil paintings is capable of distinguishing authentic works from skilled forgeries.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The painting has not been altered or restored using techniques that would obscure its original materials.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vandermeer's authenticated works from the 1640s are currently held in museum collections.

explanations.correct: The argument uses the distinctive technique as the identifying link to Vandermeer. If another painter in the 1640s also used this exact technique, the technique no longer uniquely identifies Vandermeer as the author. Negating B — another painter did use the same technique — undermines the attribution, making B necessary.
explanations.A: Whether Vandermeer painted other coastal landscapes is irrelevant. The argument attributes this specific painting to him based on technique, not subject matter.
explanations.B: Correct. The uniqueness of the technique to Vandermeer is the necessary bridge. Without it, the identification fails.
explanations.C: The argument is about layering technique analysis, not forgery detection. Whether the painting is a forgery is not addressed in the argument's premises. This introduces a new concern.
explanations.D: Alteration or restoration could be relevant as a concern, but the argument's premises already state the scientific analysis found Vandermeer's technique — so the argument implicitly treats the analysis as reliable. This is a background condition, not the core gap.
explanations.E: The location of authenticated works is irrelevant to the attribution argument. Out of scope.

difficultyReason: Environmental policy argument with a conditional chain. The argument has two premises leading to a resource conclusion. Distractors include a too-strong trap and a reversed-direction trap. The correct answer provides a necessary link in the causal chain.
stimulus: Environmental scientist: The region's primary aquifer is recharged almost entirely by snowmelt from the surrounding mountain range. Climate projections indicate that annual snowpack in those mountains will decline by 40 percent over the next 50 years. Therefore, communities that depend on the aquifer for their water supply will face serious water shortages within that period.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the scientist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The communities dependent on the aquifer will not develop alternative water sources that compensate for the reduced recharge.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A 40 percent decline in snowpack will cause a proportionally equal decline in aquifer recharge.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The climate projections cited by the scientist have been verified by at least three independent research institutions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The affected communities currently extract water from the aquifer at or near its maximum sustainable yield.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No new precipitation patterns will emerge in the mountain range that could offset the projected snowpack decline.

explanations.correct: The argument concludes that communities will face shortages. Even if the aquifer is significantly reduced, communities could avoid shortages by securing alternative water sources. Negating A — the communities do develop adequate alternative sources — means reduced aquifer recharge does not translate into shortages, collapsing the conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct. The argument must assume that the communities will not compensate for the decline through alternative sources, otherwise the shortage conclusion does not follow from reduced recharge alone.
explanations.B: Too strong and overly precise. The argument needs only that a 40% snowpack decline will cause a significant reduction in recharge sufficient to produce shortages — not a perfectly proportional decline. The exact proportionality is not required.
explanations.C: The number of institutions that verified the projections is irrelevant to whether the conclusion follows from those projections. This is an out-of-scope epistemic condition.
explanations.D: Reversed-direction trap. Even if communities are extracting well below maximum sustainable yield, a large enough reduction in recharge could still create shortages. Whether current extraction is near maximum yield is not a required bridge.
explanations.E: Too strong. The argument need not rule out every possible offsetting weather change — only that the net effect of the projected snowpack decline will be a meaningful reduction in aquifer recharge. This answer over-extends the required assumption.
